implementation_notes: Metadata is the struct tag set on the model - db:"user_name" beside each field - read by the reflection walker in sqlx (StructScan, Get, Select), which maps result columns to fields by tag or field name and skips the rest, so no hand-written per-class Scan loop exists. The same tag channel is native to Go (encoding/json, xml, validators all read it), which is why the declaration feels like language syntax, but the reader and engine are the library. Write manual rows.Scan code when a query needs per-column control or the struct is trivial; switch to GORM when the same declaration should also drive migrations.
pitfalls: Tags are strings: a typo or a column missing from the query fails at scan time with 'missing destination name', never at compile time.
Only exported fields can be set through reflection, so an unexported field is silently unmapped.
Embedded structs flatten or collide depending on tags, and duplicate column names resolve to whichever field the walker reaches first.

variants.name: GORM tags, conventions and AutoMigrate
variants.implementation_notes: GORM reads gorm:"..." tags together with conventions (ID primary key, snake_case pluralised table names, CreatedAt/UpdatedAt timestamps) to build a schema statement per model: tags override names and add constraints (primaryKey, uniqueIndex, not null, size, serializer), gorm.Model supplies the common fields, and the same metadata drives AutoMigrate and CRUD. Because one declaration feeds both migration and mapping this is the closest Go gets to a framework-owned metadata store, at the price of inference: table and column names follow conventions until tagged.
pitfalls: Convention inference means renaming a struct or field changes the table or column; without explicit tags an innocent refactor silently targets different SQL.
Zero values are skipped on Updates unless Select is used, so 'leave unchanged' and 'set to zero' get confused.
Hooks and soft deletes (gorm.DeletedAt) add behaviour to the mapping that is invisible in the struct tags.

variants.name: ent schema-as-code + generated typed clients
variants.idiom_name: ent.Schema Go code compiled by entc
variants.implementation_notes: The metadata store here is ordinary Go code: an ent.Schema type whose Fields, Edges and Indexes methods declare field types, relations and indexes, with schema annotations supplying database-specific options such as a custom table name. The entc generator is the reader - it loads the schema definitions and generates the typed entity structs, builders and migration code - so mismatches between declared schema and generated code are caught at generation time and the resulting API is type-safe. Use it when compile-time-checked mapping matters and running the generator in the build is acceptable.
pitfalls: Schema and generated code are two states: editing the schema without re-running the generator leaves the old mapping in place.
Reserved schema names and annotations are enforced by the generator, so a schema type may be rejected long after it was written.
